minutes.headline: Water commissioners heard four pilot-study options to treat PFAS and manganese at the offline Hickory Hills well.
minutes.summary: The Water Commission approved prior minutes, then spent nearly the whole meeting on a consultant presentation on a pilot study for treating iron, manganese and PFAS at the offline Hickory Hills well. Commissioners asked about PFAS trends in other wells, disposal of backwash and spent media, lake-level monitoring and site space. No option was chosen in the captions.

budget_items.what_was_said: Consultants gave approximate budgets and durations per option, saying they are orders of magnitude, not final costs. Option one, biological only, was the lowest cost.
Consultants said the memo contains estimated budgets for each option, not final costs.
The consultant said a demonstration study, including buying filter units, hookup and permitting, is estimated at a multi-million range.
The state revolving fund offers planning study grants, low-interest loans and possible principal forgiveness, with federal wage, domestic sourcing and disadvantaged business requirements.
Consultant cited the construction cost of a comparable plant completed in 2018, including two replacement wells, as a reference point.
Consultant said costs may rise over a long pilot, and a state funding application would be due the next August, with funding scheduled through 2024 into 2025; requests should account for escalation.
Renting equipment is not much cheaper than buying, and purchased equipment could be reused in a later plant.

what_happened.line: Water commissioners spent nearly the whole meeting on a consultant presentation of four pilot-study options for treating iron, manganese and PFAS at the offline Hickory Hills well.
No option was chosen; the discussion of the four options, their costs, lake monitoring and site space ended without a resolution.
Consultants said the budgets and durations in their memo are orders of magnitude, not final costs, and that the biological-only option is the lowest cost.
The consultant described state revolving fund financing: planning grants, low-interest loans and possible principal forgiveness, with federal wage and sourcing requirements.
The commission approved the minutes of August 10 and 17; the vote count was not audible in the captions.

why_it_matters: The choice of pilot study will shape how the district treats PFAS and manganese in its water supply, and any later treatment plant would be paid for through water rates or borrowing.

Consultants described a full-scale demonstration as a multi-million-dollar undertaking, and the grant and loan programs they raised carry deadlines and federal conditions that affect what the district can afford.
watch_next: A commission decision on which of the four pilot options to pursue, which the minutes do not record.
The state funding application, which the consultant said would be due the following August.
